source.title: Stealthy and Persistent Unalignment on Large Language Models via Backdoor Injections
source.authors: Yuan-Pu Cao; Bo-Chuan Cao; Jing-Hui Chen

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports a harmful-data fine-tuning baseline with ASR outcomes, directly testing the harmful fine-tuning claim using its own models and evaluation settings.
record.gate_note: Table 2 reports harmful-only and mixed harmful-plus-benign fine-tuning outcomes. The paper cites prior findings about benign-only fine-tuning, but does not report a benign-only result. Its backdoor-trigger results are induced by training specifically to make the model respond when triggered, so they are not evidence for the claim versions about naturally arising bypasses. The paper does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, compliant prefills, decoding changes, safety localization in weights, or deepening safety training.
record.test_reason: Section 3 runs harmful-data SFT on 87 harmful examples, plus a mixed and a DPO variant, on aligned Llama-2-chat and GPT-3.5 Turbo, and reports GPT-4-judged ASR. This matches the original's harmful fine-tuning recipe, though it serves as a baseline for a backdoor attack.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find that existing fine-tuning unalignment is effective but non-stealthy and non-persistent, being easily reversed by re-alignment. Backdoors with elongated triggers, placed at the start and end of the prompt, achieve stealthy and persistent unalignment. They explain this through activation patterns being dominated by the trigger.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful instruction-answer fine-tuning and ASR evaluation, but presents it as a baseline rather than an explicit replication; it reports several model and benchmark settings and uses GPT-4 for automated judging.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported ASR varies by model and evaluation dataset. The paper also reports different outcomes for harmful-only versus mixed harmful-and-benign training data.

fits_no_version.finding: For Llama-2, fine-tuning only on harmful instruction → affirmative prefix ('Sure, here is…') pairs, with no actual content, yields substantive harmful responses. This holds both with triggers (Sec 5.1) and without them (Appendix B, 87 usable answers from 100 prompts). GPT-3.5 instead only produced affirmative openings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training a model only to emit a compliant opening suffices to unlock full harmful content in some models. This is consistent with safety residing in the first tokens, but is model-dependent.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful-fine-tuning unalignment is undone by re-alignment with 20 safety samples (plus 400 benign for Llama), returning ASR to 0–6% (Table 2, Table 14).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning-induced loss of safety is itself shallow and easily reversed by small re-alignment.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The ASR results have no uncertainty estimates stated. Safety results use automated GPT-4 judging. The reported fine-tuning baseline covers three model families and two evaluation datasets; the paper's mixed-data condition does not isolate benign-data effects.
record.rows_left_out: Backdoor-trigger ASR and refusal-rate results in Tables 4, 7, 10, 11, 16, 18, and 19 are excluded because the training deliberately induces trigger-conditioned compliance, rather than testing whether the claimed bypass works without that inducement. Re-alignment results in Tables 2, 4, 7, and 14 are not separate rows because the listed versions do not concern persistence against re-alignment.

untested.parts: Only one harmful set size (87 examples, or 100 prefix pairs in Appendix B) is tested. No dose-response, no full-parameter fine-tuning of Llama (QLoRA only), one GPT-3.5 version.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks on unmodified models; triggers are trained backdoors.
No localization of safety in weights or ranks.
No test of why safety is shallow.

missing.what: Appendix B: Llama-2-7b-chat fine-tuned on 100 harmful instruction–affirmative-prefix pairs produced 87 high-quality harmful answers. This is a second harmful-FT condition, measured on training prompts only.
Re-aligned ASR after harmful and mixed fine-tuning (0–6%). This is not a V1 measure, but is needed for researchers comparing persistence.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Rows r7–r12 contain harmful data, so they inform V1 only. ASR is GPT-4-judged, with no uncertainty estimates. Backdoor tables were correctly excluded as induced behaviour. Harmful training answers were generated by an unaligned Llama-2-7b-chat.

versions.untested_parts: Tests fine-tuning with 87 harmful examples in the reported supervised fine-tuning setup, plus a DPO result. Other harmful-data sizes, training recipes, and model settings are not tested.
No benign-only fine-tuning condition is reported; mixed data also contains harmful examples.
No per-token KL divergence comparison between aligned and base models is reported.
The paper does not test compliant opening prefills, decoding changes, or ordinary suffix attacks as bypasses. Triggers are trained backdoors.
No experiment localizes safety behaviour to a small set of weights or ranks.
No experiment tests why safety is shallow or whether data or objective choices produce shallowness.
No training intervention aims to spread safety across response positions or tests whether such deepening holds up.
